The Frontier Model Market Landscape: Who Builds, Trains, Serves and Sells the Models

Behind every AI product is a stack of companies: labs that build models, open-weight challengers, the software that trains and serves them, the hubs that distribute them, and the chips and clouds they run on. This visual deep dive maps each layer as of September 2026 — with verified model line-ups and prices, an interactive cost calculator, a build-vs-buy break-even chart and a runnable cost model.

How to read this: this market moves monthly. Model names, dates and prices below were checked against provider pages and reporting in September 2026 and are linked in References; always confirm current prices before budgeting. Interactive figures compute from the stated numbers; anything that is an assumption (GPU rental rates, throughput) is labelled and adjustable.

01 The Market Stack

From a model's creation to its use, five layers each have their own companies, business models and competitive dynamics. Click a layer:

▶ Five layers, from model to end user The glowing dot follows a model from the lab to real-world use.

02 Frontier Model Providers (Closed / Proprietary)

Closed providers sell access, not weights: through an API, their own apps, and the big clouds' model catalogs. Their line-ups have converged on the same shape — a flagship, a balanced workhorse and a fast, cheap tier, most with million-token context and adjustable reasoning effort.

OpenAI
  • GPT-6 Astra — new flagship; approved users 3 Sep 2026, general availability the next day; ~1.05M context; $10 / $50
  • GPT-5.6 family (July 2026) in three tiers: Sol (frontier), Terra (balanced), Luna (fast, low cost)
  • Via API, ChatGPT and Amazon Web Services
Anthropic
  • Claude Fable 5.1 (1 Sep 2026) — $10 / $50
  • Claude Opus 5.5 (22 Sep 2026) — $4 / $20; 1M context
  • Claude Sonnet 5 — $2 / $10 · Claude Haiku 4.5 — $1 / $5
  • Claude Mythos 5.1 — restricted to trusted-access programmes
  • Via API, Claude apps, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry
Google
  • Gemini 3.1 Pro — current Pro model; 1M context; natively multimodal
  • Gemini 3.5 Flash (19 May 2026) — $1.50 / $9; default in the Gemini app
  • Gemini Omni — any-input-to-video generation model (I/O 2026)
  • Gemini 3.5 Pro — announced, still unreleased as of late August 2026
Meta
  • Muse Spark (April 2026) — Meta's first proprietary frontier model, from Meta Superintelligence Labs; API $1.25 / $4.25
  • Also open weights — see section 03

Prices are list prices in US dollars per million input / output tokens as of September 2026. Caching and batch discounts can cut effective cost substantially.

▶ What would your workload cost? Monthly API cost at list prices. Pick a preset or set your own.
Cost = requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 1,000,000. Agents are input-heavy (they re-read context every step), so input price and prompt caching matter more than the headline output price.

03 The Open-Weight Ecosystem

Open-weight models publish their parameters so anyone can download, fine-tune and host them — the basis of self-hosting, on-device AI and most academic research. In 2026 the largest open models are giant sparse mixtures-of-experts, and China's labs release many of the strongest.

▶ Total vs active parameters Each dot is an open-weight model (log scales). Hover or tap for details.
Tap a model. Dots on the diagonal are dense (every parameter active); far below it are sparse MoE models.
Meta
  • Muse Glimmer 30B (August 2026) — dense, Apache 2.0, runs on one GPU, tuned for agents and tool use
  • Llama 4 Scout and Maverick (April 2025) — MoE, Llama 4 Community License
  • Meta's 2026 strategy is hybrid: closed Muse Spark plus open Glimmer
DeepSeek
  • DeepSeek-V4 (April 2026) — V4-Pro 1.6T total / 49B active; 1M context
  • DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (September 2026) — 552B total, ~8B / 16B active
  • Strong reasoning and coding; detailed technical reports
Alibaba · Qwen
  • Qwen3.5 (February 2026) — open Qwen3.5-397B-A17B; proprietary Qwen3.5-Plus
  • Qwen3.8 (August 2026) — open Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, the first open Max-class Qwen, and dense Qwen3.8-27B (Apache 2.0)
Mistral AI
  • Mistral 3 (December 2025) — Mistral Large 3, a 675B-total / 41B-active MoE, plus dense 14B, 8B and 3B models
  • All Apache 2.0
Open weights ≠ open source: most releases publish weights and a licence but not the training data or full training code. Licences differ — Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive; others (such as the Llama licence) add conditions. Check the licence before building a product on a model.

04 The Training Software Stack

Almost every model — closed or open — is trained with a small set of frameworks that implement the parallelism and memory techniques from Part 2:

PyTorch (FSDP)The default deep-learning framework in research and industry; Fully Sharded Data Parallel shards parameters, gradients and optimizer state.
DeepSpeedMicrosoft's library: ZeRO sharding stages, offload to CPU/NVMe, memory and throughput optimizations.
NVIDIA Megatron-CoreTensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism for transformer training at the largest scales.
JAXGoogle's framework (with XLA): used for Gemini and in several large training pipelines, particularly on TPUs.
NVIDIA Transformer EngineMixed-precision (FP8, and FP4 on Blackwell) transformer kernels for higher training throughput.

05 Inference and Serving Engines

Serving engines implement continuous batching, paged KV cache, speculative decoding and quantization (Part 2). The open-source field has consolidated around a few engines. Pick what you need:

▶ Which engine fits? A simplified guide — most teams benchmark two or three on their own workload.
EngineStrengthsNotes
vLLMHigh-throughput serving, PagedAttention, continuous batching, OpenAI-compatible API, broad hardware supportThe most widely used open engine
SGLangFast serving for complex programs; RadixAttention prefix caching; strong on agents and structured outputPopular for large MoE deployments
TensorRT-LLMNVIDIA-optimized kernels, quantization, in-flight batchingOften run under NVIDIA Dynamo or Triton
llama.cppLightweight local inference on CPUs, Apple silicon and consumer GPUs; GGUF quantizationBehind many desktop apps (e.g. Ollama)
Hugging Face TGIProduction serving pioneerIn maintenance mode since December 2025; Hugging Face now recommends vLLM or SGLang
Commercial platformsManaged inference, autoscaling, multi-model serving, monitoringTogether AI, Fireworks, Baseten and the clouds' own services

07 Cloud and Accelerator Infrastructure

The whole market runs on a handful of chip families. NVIDIA dominates, but every hyperscaler now also designs its own accelerator, and frontier labs spread workloads across several to secure capacity and price.

▶ Accelerator generations Pick a vendor. Status as of September 2026.
Hyperscale clouds
  • AWS — broadest AI services, Bedrock
  • Microsoft Azure — Foundry, OpenAI models
  • Google Cloud — Vertex AI, TPUs
  • Oracle Cloud (OCI)
Specialist GPU clouds
  • CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale
  • Together AI (GPU clusters + inference)
  • High-performance clusters, on-demand GPUs
Why it matters
  • Compute is the largest cost of training and serving
  • Capacity is often reserved years ahead
  • Software stacks (CUDA, ROCm, XLA, Neuron) shape portability
Documented examples: NVIDIA said on 21 July 2026 that Vera Rubin was in full production and shipping to customers including OpenAI, CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Meta. Google's Ironwood (TPU7x) reached general availability with Anthropic as the anchor customer. AWS made Trainium3 UltraServers (up to 144 chips) generally available in December 2025. AMD launched the Instinct MI455X and its Helios rack in 2026.

08 Build vs Buy

Every organization chooses a point on a spectrum from "call an API" to "train our own model". Each step down gives more control and data isolation, and costs more engineering:

OptionExamplesControlCostSpeed to useOps burdenData governanceTypical use
Closed APIOpenAI, Anthropic, Google GeminiLowPay per tokenFastLowProvider handles (contracts, regions, zero-retention options)Most applications, rapid deployment
Self-hosted open weightsDeepSeek-V4, Qwen3.8, Mistral 3, Muse GlimmerHighInfrastructureMediumHighYour infrastructureCustom deployment, full control, regulated data
Fine-tuned, hosted open modelQwen or Mistral on a cloud platformMediumPer token or per hourMediumMediumYour data in your cloud accountDomain adaptation
Train from scratchCustom modelVery highVery highSlowVery highYour infrastructureFrontier research, unique capabilities

The money question — when does self-hosting beat an API? — depends on volume. A GPU cluster costs the same whether it is busy or idle; an API costs per token. Move the sliders:

▶ Break-even: API vs self-hosted Monthly cost as volume grows. GPU figures are adjustable assumptions, not quotes.
Self-hosted cost = replicas × 8 GPUs × $/hour × 730 hours, where replicas = ⌈monthly tokens ÷ (tokens/s × utilization × 3600 × 730)⌉ — a staircase, because you pay for whole replicas. Excludes engineering salaries, and assumes the open model is good enough for the task, which is the bigger question.

The same model as a script, using September 2026 list prices and the default assumptions above:

"""What does a workload cost on each frontier API — and when does self-hosting an open model win?

API list prices (USD per 1M tokens, input / output) as published in September 2026. Self-hosting uses
stated assumptions you should replace with your own quotes and benchmarks. Standard library only.
"""
import math

API = {  # model: (input $/1M, output $/1M)
    "GPT-6 Astra":        (10.00, 50.00),
    "Claude Fable 5.1":   (10.00, 50.00),
    "Claude Opus 5.5":    ( 4.00, 20.00),
    "Claude Sonnet 5":    ( 2.00, 10.00),
    "Gemini 3.5 Flash":   ( 1.50,  9.00),
    "Muse Spark (Meta)":  ( 1.25,  4.25),
    "Claude Haiku 4.5":   ( 1.00,  5.00),
}
WORKLOADS = {  # name: (requests per month, input tokens, output tokens per request)
    "support chatbot":    (2_000_000, 1_500, 300),
    "RAG over documents": (  500_000, 8_000, 500),
    "coding agent":       (   50_000, 60_000, 4_000),
}

def monthly(model, reqs, tin, tout):
    pin, pout = API[model]
    return reqs * (tin * pin + tout * pout) / 1e6

print("Monthly API cost (list prices, no caching or batch discounts)\n")
print(f"   {'model':<20}" + "".join(f"{w:>22}" for w in WORKLOADS))
for m in API:
    print(f"   {m:<20}" + "".join(f"{'$' + format(round(monthly(m, *w)), ','):>22}" for w in WORKLOADS.values()))

# Self-hosting an open-weight model: assumptions, not quotes
GPU_HOUR, GPUS, TOK_PER_S, UTIL = 2.50, 8, 12_000, 0.5     # $/GPU-hour, GPUs per replica, total tokens/s per replica, average utilization
per_replica = GPU_HOUR * GPUS * 730                          # 730 hours per month
capacity = TOK_PER_S * UTIL * 3600 * 730                     # tokens a replica serves per month
print(f"\nSelf-hosted open model: {GPUS} GPUs x ${GPU_HOUR}/h = ${per_replica:,.0f}/month per replica, "
      f"~{capacity / 1e9:.1f}B tokens/month at {UTIL:.0%} utilization (assumptions)")
for w, (reqs, tin, tout) in WORKLOADS.items():
    toks = reqs * (tin + tout)
    replicas = max(1, math.ceil(toks / capacity))
    self_cost = replicas * per_replica
    cheapest = min(API, key=lambda m: monthly(m, reqs, tin, tout))
    print(f"   {w:<20} {toks / 1e9:>6.1f}B tokens -> {replicas} replica(s) ${self_cost:>9,.0f}   vs cheapest API here "
          f"({cheapest}) ${monthly(cheapest, reqs, tin, tout):>9,.0f}")
print(f"\nAt full replicas, self-hosting costs ${per_replica / capacity * 1e6:.2f} per 1M tokens. Blended API price for the chatbot mix,")
print("and the monthly volume where one replica breaks even with it:")
reqs, tin, tout = WORKLOADS["support chatbot"]
for m, (pin, pout) in API.items():
    blended = (tin * pin + tout * pout) / (tin + tout)
    print(f"   {m:<20} ${blended:>6.2f} per 1M   break-even at {per_replica / blended * 1e6 / 1e9:>5.1f}B tokens/month")
print("\nSelf-hosting also needs engineers, on-call, evaluation and a model good enough for the task.")

Self-hosting also needs engineers, on-call, evaluation and a model good enough for the task.

With these assumptions, all three example workloads are cheaper on an API. Self-hosting pays off above a few billion tokens a month — sooner against flagship prices, later against small models — or when control, data residency or customization matter more than price.

The market in one paragraph
In September 2026, three closed labs — OpenAI (GPT-6 Astra), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5) and Google (Gemini 3.x) — sell the frontier through APIs and the major clouds, with Meta now among them via Muse Spark. A strong open-weight tier led by DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Meta publishes models of 500B to 2.4T parameters that anyone can host. Underneath, a few frameworks train almost everything, vLLM and SGLang serve most open models, Hugging Face distributes them, and NVIDIA — increasingly alongside TPUs, Trainium and AMD — supplies the compute. Hosting and standard serving are commoditizing; frontier capability, reasoning, proprietary data and enterprise trust are where value concentrates. For most buyers the rational default is an API, with self-hosting reserved for large volumes, strict data control or deep customization.

⚠️ Notes

Corrections to the source infographic, checked against provider pages and reporting in September 2026: (1) OpenAI — the flagship is now GPT-6 Astra (released 3–4 September 2026), and the GPT-5.6 family's tiers are named Sol, Terra and Luna, not "GPT-5.6-mini" and "-nano"; (2) Anthropic — there is no "Claude Haiku 5"; the current small model is Claude Haiku 4.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 is restricted to trusted-access programmes rather than generally available; (3) Meta — the infographic lists only Llama 4, but Meta's 2026 releases are Muse Spark (proprietary) and Muse Glimmer 30B (open weights, Apache 2.0), so Meta now sits in both the closed and open columns; (4) Qwen — the latest open releases are Qwen3.5 (February) and Qwen3.8 (August 2026), beyond the "Qwen3, Qwen3.5" shown; (5) Hugging Face TGI has been in maintenance mode since December 2025; (6) accelerators — "TPUs (v5e, v6)" is out of date (Ironwood / TPU7x is generally available), "Inferentia 3" does not exist (the current chip is Inferentia2; AWS's newest is Trainium3), and NVIDIA's current generations are Blackwell and Vera Rubin, which began shipping in July 2026. Gemini 3.5 Pro, announced in May, was still unreleased in late August 2026. Market share figures are deliberately omitted: they are rarely published and hard to verify.
